Energy Beyond the Grid: Gas Turbines, Nuclear Restarts and the Race for Private Power

The grid cannot connect new gigawatts fast enough for AI. So the builders are bringing their own power: fleets of gas turbines next to data centres, shut-down nuclear plants brought back to life, deals for reactors that do not exist yet, and fuel cells by the hundred megawatts. This guide compares every option on speed, cost, carbon and risk, follows the biggest projects, and asks who pays when data centres leave the grid, or stay on it.

⚡ Why leave the grid?

The Power Bottleneck explained why AI's appetite for electricity collides with grids built for slow growth. In 2026 the collision is visible in prices and queues. In PJM, the grid operator serving 13 US states and Washington DC, the capacity price that pays power plants to be available rose from $28.92 per megawatt-day for 2024/25 to $329.17 for 2026/27. The 2028/29 auction cleared at the federal price cap of $325 and still came up 6,831 MW short of the reliability target. PJM's market monitor attributes $6.3 billion, 38% of the latest auction's $16.4 billion cost, to data centres.

Waiting years for a grid connection is not an option for companies racing to train the next model. So developers have begun building their own power plants on site, known as behind-the-meter generation, and signing deals to revive or build nuclear capacity.

🔥 Gas: the fast answer

Natural gas turbines can be installed in months to a couple of years, run around the clock and sit right next to the servers. Cleanview's 2026 tracker counts about 101 GW of behind-the-meter gas generation announced for US data centres, of which more than 57 GW has disclosed equipment orders and about 7 GW is under construction. Texas alone accounts for about 38 GW. Only around 2 GW was actually operating by mid-2026, most of it at one company.

📉 From announcement to electrons

US behind-the-meter gas for data centres, gigawatts. Announced totals include speculative projects.

Cleanview, "Bypassing the Grid" (mid-2026). Operating figure: ~2 GW across four projects, mostly xAI.

xAI, Memphis
The pioneer. Colossus 1 and 2 near Memphis account for about 1,498 MW of operating gas turbine capacity, with dozens of temporary mobile turbines added at the Southaven site across the state line. Cleanview projects total behind-the-meter capacity of 2.8–3.2 GW by the end of 2026. The turbines have drawn local opposition over air pollution.
Stargate, Abilene
Crusoe's campus for OpenAI in Abilene, Texas, with power demand of about 1.2 GW, uses aeroderivative turbines adapted from jet engines, which start fast and come in smaller units.
Others
Developers in Texas, Ohio, Pennsylvania and the Southwest plan gas plants sized from hundreds of megawatts to several gigawatts, often with the option to connect to the grid later.
🚧 The catches Turbines are sold out: GE Vernova, Siemens Energy and Mitsubishi reported lead times of 24 months or more for new orders (as of late 2025), and GE Vernova expects to reach about 20 GW a year of gas turbine output in 2026. Permits: Nebius has struggled to obtain an air permit for a 400 MW on-site gas plant in New Jersey. Climate laws: in states such as Virginia, on-site gas raises questions about whether data centres can sidestep renewable-energy mandates. Emissions and fuel price risk follow the plant for decades.

♻️ Nuclear restarts: bringing plants back

The fastest route to large amounts of clean, round-the-clock power is to restart reactors that closed for economic reasons. Three US plants are in progress, each backed by a tech company's long-term contract and federal loans: the Department of Energy has committed $4.42 billion across them. As of mid-October 2026, none had returned to service.

🔬 Small modular reactors and advanced nuclear

Small modular reactors (SMRs) promise factory-built units of tens to a few hundred megawatts that could sit near data centres. Big tech companies have signed a wave of deals, but none of these reactors is running yet, and most first units target 2030 or later.

🔋 Fuel cells and the rest

Fuel cells convert natural gas into electricity chemically, without combustion, so they emit almost no local air pollutants (though still CO₂), need no air permit in many places and can be installed in modules within months. Bloom Energy has become a major supplier: a 20-year, $2.65 billion agreement with utility AEP signed in January 2026 covers an initial 100 MW with an option to expand to 1 GW, and an April 2026 agreement with Oracle is reported at 2.45–2.8 GW (sources conflict). Brookfield has committed billions to finance Bloom deployments.

Batteries smooth the spiky power draw of training runs and provide backup. Solar and wind with storage, bought through long-term power purchase agreements, remain the cheapest new energy, but cannot alone guarantee round-the-clock supply. Geothermal (including new enhanced geothermal) offers firm clean power at small scale today.

🏛️ Grid politics: who pays?

📈 PJM capacity prices

Clearing price, $ per megawatt-day, by delivery year.

PJM auction results via IEEFA, Enel and the market monitor (Utility Dive). 2028/29 cleared at the $325 cap, 6,831 MW short.

Capacity costs flow into everyone's electricity bills, so the question of who pays for data-centre growth has become political. Regulators are trying to write rules for data centres that build their own generation or co-locate next to existing power plants, which can take clean power off the grid that households rely on.

Dec 2025
FERC found PJM's tariff unjust and unreasonable for lacking clear co-location rules and ordered reforms.
Apr 2026
FERC partially approved PJM's compliance package, rejecting its revised definition of co-located load.
Jun 2026
FERC issued show-cause orders requiring all six US regional grid operators to justify or reform their rules for large loads, rather than adopting one national rule; the large-load rulemaking docket (RM26-4) remains open.
💡 The trade-off Data centres that bring their own power relieve pressure on the grid but may lock in decades of gas emissions and leave the grid's fixed costs to fewer customers. Data centres that stay on the grid share the system but push up capacity prices for everyone. Most rule-makers are converging on a middle path: let large loads connect faster if they bring generation, accept curtailment in emergencies, or pay their full share of new infrastructure.

🎛️ Power a 1 GW AI campus

Choose how many megawatts come from each source. Timings and emission factors are rough, illustrative values.

Assumptions: 1 GW load at 85% average use. Emission factors (t CO₂/MWh): gas turbines ~0.45, fuel cells on natural gas ~0.37, average grid mix ~0.37, clean PPA and nuclear ~0. Time to power: fuel cells ~1 yr, gas ~2 yrs (turbine queues), grid connection ~4–7 yrs, nuclear restart ~2027–29, SMR ~2030+.

🕰️ Timeline

2024 · Constellation and Microsoft agree to restart Three Mile Island Unit 1 (renamed Crane); Google–Kairos and Amazon–X-energy SMR deals.
2024–25 · xAI installs gas turbines to power Colossus in Memphis.
2025 · Crusoe builds Stargate Abilene with on-site aeroderivative turbines; Google and NextEra agree to restart Duane Arnold.
Dec 2025 · FERC orders PJM to set clear co-location rules.
Jan 2026 · Meta–Oklo prepayment (1.2 GW, Ohio) and Meta–TerraPower deal; Bloom–AEP $2.65B fuel-cell agreement.
Mar 2026 · TerraPower's Kemmerer construction permit.
Jun 2026 · FERC show-cause orders to all six regional grid operators on large loads.
Aug 2026 · Palisades begins loading fuel; a tilted assembly stalls the process.
Sep 2026 · DOE closes up to $1.9B loan for Duane Arnold; NRC final environmental assessment for Crane; TVA Clinch River construction approval.
13 Oct 2026 · NRC approves licence amendment to move Palisades' tilted fuel assembly.

🔭 What to watch

  • Palisades and Crane: the first restarts to return to service, and whether Crane's grid connection is really delayed to 2031.
  • Turbine supply: GE Vernova, Siemens Energy and Mitsubishi capacity expansions, and lead times.
  • Air permits and local opposition to on-site gas, from Memphis to New Jersey.
  • FERC and grid operators' large-load rules, and PJM's next capacity auction.
  • First SMR construction at TVA Clinch River, Kemmerer and X-energy sites, and Oklo's licence application.
  • Off-Earth options: see Data Centers in Space for the most radical way to escape the grid.
🎯 The bottom line AI's power needs have outrun the grid, so the industry is building a private energy system alongside it. In the near term that means gas: turbines and fuel cells are the only options that deliver gigawatts within two years, at the cost of emissions and fierce competition for equipment. Nuclear is the long-term bet: restarts arrive from 2027 at the earliest, SMRs around 2030 and later. Meanwhile the grid's own capacity prices have soared, and regulators are rewriting the rules on who pays. The companies that secure power fastest will train and serve the most AI.

🔢 Reading the numbers

  • Gas totals (101 GW announced) include speculative projects; only ~2 GW was operating by mid-2026.
  • xAI capacity comes from Cleanview's tracker; turbine counts change frequently.
  • Restart dates are company targets and have slipped before; Palisades' 2026 return is now unlikely per one analysis.
  • SMR timelines differ between sources (Kairos 2030 vs 2035) and are very uncertain.
  • Fuel-cell deal sizes (Oracle 2.45 vs 2.8 GW) conflict between aggregator sources.
  • Ratings and simulator values are illustrative.
